name: Monobenzone

lead: Monobenzone is a topical drug that permanently removes pigment from skin. Its approved use is in people with widespread vitiligo, where it evens out the remaining normal skin to match the depigmented patches.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a permanent skin whitener, with members weighing whether to go paler than their natural tone. Laboratory studies report that tyrosinase in melanocytes converts it into reactive quinones that bind cellular proteins and trigger an immune response against pigmented cells, leading to lasting loss of melanocytes. No trial has tested it for cosmetic lightening of normal skin.

paras: In its approved use it is a prescription cream applied to remaining pigmented skin in extensive vitiligo under medical supervision. Forum threads also describe online and gray-market purchasing for cosmetic use.

Reported effects include irritation, contact dermatitis, allergic reactions and depigmentation at untreated sites. The effect is described as permanent and does not reverse after stopping. It is prescription-only in the US, and use outside vitiligo is off-label.

angle.text: A prescription cream that destroys pigment cells so skin ends up uniformly pale; approved for extensive vitiligo. Forums discuss it as a permanent whitener, though use outside vitiligo is off-label and the effect is described as irreversible.

lead: Monobenzone, also called monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH) or 4-(benzyloxy)phenol, is a topical depigmenting agent. In the United States it is a prescription-only drug used to permanently remove remaining skin pigment in people with extensive vitiligo, so that the unaffected skin matches the depigmented patches [1][2]. Unlike milder skin-lightening ingredients, its effect is described in the literature as irreversible, because it leads to the loss of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells [3][4].

Laboratory research has found that monobenzone is converted by tyrosinase inside melanocytes into reactive quinone species that bind to proteins and make pigmented cells a target for the immune system, rather than only blocking pigment production [3][5][6]. That immune mechanism has also been investigated in melanoma, in a small phase 2a trial combining monobenzone with imiquimod [7].

In looksmaxxing communities, monobenzone is discussed as a 'permanent skin whitener' and as a product that some members consider using to lighten their overall skin tone, with ordering from online pharmacies and gray-market sellers described in forum threads [8][9]. No published trial has evaluated it as a cosmetic lightener in people without vitiligo, and its depigmentation is not reversible once established [1][2].
infobox: Prescription-only in the US; unscheduled in Canada [1]

paras: The recognised medical use is depigmentation of normally pigmented skin in people whose vitiligo already covers a large share of the body, commonly described as more than half of the body surface area [1][2]. The aim is an even skin tone once repigmentation treatments have failed or are unsuitable [2]. Clinical guidelines for vitiligo describe depigmentation as an option for extensive disease [10].
Monobenzone has also been explored in melanoma immunotherapy research, which is a separate research use and not an appearance use [7].

Human research on monobenzone is limited and centres on its use as a depigmenting agent in people with extensive vitiligo. Evidence-based guidelines for vitiligo treatment have described depigmentation as an option for widespread disease [10], and a 1985 report in Archives of Dermatology described dermatitis arising from monobenzone applications in patients with active vitiligo [11].

A 2018 phase 2a trial examined monobenzone combined with imiquimod in patients with cutaneous melanoma metastases. It reported anti-melanoma immune responses and local regression of some metastases, and it concerned cancer immunotherapy rather than cosmetic depigmentation [7].

Most mechanistic work, including studies of tyrosinase haptenation, melanocyte-specific immunity and a mouse model of monobenzone-induced vitiligo, was done in cell and animal systems rather than in clinical trials [3][4][12]. A secondary summary reports that depigmentation was achieved in a large majority of selected patients with severe vitiligo, but it does not rest on a large randomised trial [2].

Reported effects include skin irritation and contact dermatitis, which have been described in people with active vitiligo [11]. Reference text describing the drug also reports allergic reactions and depigmentation at sites distant from where it was applied, including covered skin [2].

The central feature is irreversibility: once melanocytes are lost, pigment does not return, which is why the product label and clinicians treat the decision as permanent and associate the drug with sun-protection needs afterwards [2]. Dermatology guidance also stresses psychological readiness and expectations before treatment [2].

Monobenzone is a pro-hapten: tyrosinase in melanocytes oxidises it to a reactive ortho-quinone that conjugates with thiols and tyrosinase protein [5][6]. A 2011 study reported that this haptenation, together with melanosome oxidative stress, makes pigmented cells more immunogenic and drives T-cell responses against melanocyte antigens [3]. A 2016 study in mice described a long-lasting, melanocyte-specific response dependent on natural killer cells [4]. A mouse model of vitiligo induced by monobenzone has also been described [12]. A review frames the process as moving from enzymatic blockade to autoimmunity [5].
Monobenzone is the monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, a white to colourless crystalline solid that dissolves in alcohol but hardly in water [1][2].

Wikipedia lists monobenzone as prescription-only in the United States and unscheduled in Canada [1]. A brand-name cream, Benoquin, is described in a Grokipedia article as discontinued, with compounded 20% preparations available [2].

Threads on looksmax.org include members asking whether monobenzone is worth using to become paler, weighing it against keeping a natural tan [9]. Other threads ask whether any members have tried it as a permanent skin whitener [13]. Some posts describe ordering the cream from overseas online pharmacies, and members also speculate about whether others' appearance reflects skin-lightening products [8]. Community discussion often includes commentary about identity and skin colour; this article records only that such discussions exist.

lore.intro: Monobenzone appears in looksmaxxing forums as a permanent skin-whitening option and is often mentioned alongside other lightening products [8][9].
